facts.fact_text: The applicant was a member of a group of aliens without residence permits.
The applicant was a spokeswoman for a group of aliens without residence permits.

In 1996, the group of aliens without residence permits decided to take collective action to draw attention to the difficulties they were having in obtaining a review of their immigration status in France.
The campaign of the group of aliens without residence permits culminated with the occupation of St Bernard's Church in Paris on 28 June 1996.
The group that occupied St Bernard's Church in Paris on 28 June 1996 numbered approximately two hundred illegal immigrants.
The applicant's daughter joined the applicant as one of the occupiers of St Bernard's Church in Paris.
The movement occupying St Bernard's Church was known as the 'St Bernard sans papiers' movement.
The 'St Bernard sans papiers' movement was supported by several human-rights organisations.

Some activists from the human-rights organisations supporting the 'St Bernard sans papiers' movement decided to sleep on the premises of St Bernard's Church in a show of solidarity with the occupiers' predicament.
On 22 August 1996, the Paris Commissioner of Police signed an order for the total evacuation of St Bernard's Church in Paris.
The morning following the signing of the evacuation order (23 August 1996), the police carried out the evacuation of St Bernard's Church.
Police officers arrived at St Bernard's Church at 6.30 a.m. on 23 August 1996.
The police entered St Bernard's Church at 7.56 a.m. on 23 August 1996.
All the occupants of St Bernard's Church were stopped and questioned by police during the evacuation on 23 August 1996.
Police assembled all the dark-skinned occupants of St Bernard's Church, apart from those on hunger strike, and sent them by coach to an aliens' detention centre at Vincennes.
At 9.55 a.m. on 23 August 1996, the applicant was taken into custody and informed of her rights pursuant to Articles 63-2 and 63-4 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
The Paris Criminal Court sentenced the applicant to two months' imprisonment, suspended.
On 22 August 1996, the Paris Commissioner of Police signed an order for the total evacuation of St Bernard's Church in Paris.

The checkpoint at St Bernard's Church was set up on the basis of Article 78-2, subparagraphs 1 and 3, of the Code of Criminal Procedure and Article 8, subparagraphs 2 and 3, of the Ordinance of 2 November 1945.

Article 78-2, subparagraph 1, of the French Code of Criminal Procedure provides that senior police officers and ordinary police officers acting on the orders of senior police officers who are accountable for their actions may invite any person to prove his or her identity by any means if there are grounds for suspecting that he or she has committed or attempted to commit an offence.

Article 78-2, subparagraph 1, of the French Code of Criminal Procedure provides that senior police officers and ordinary police officers acting on the orders of senior police officers who are accountable for their actions may invite any person to prove his or her identity by any means if there are grounds for suspecting that he or she is preparing to commit a serious crime (crime) or other major offence (délit), may be able to provide information that will assist in the investigation of a serious crime or other major offence, or is wanted by a judicial authority.

Article L. 2512-13 of the General Code of the Territorial Authorities provides that in the City of Paris the Commissioner of Police shall have the powers and prerogatives conferred on him by the Ordinance of the Consuls of 12 Messidor, Year VIII, determining the functions of the Paris Commissioner of Police, by the amendments made thereto, and by Articles L. 2512-7, L. 2512-14 and L. 2512-17.

Article L. 2512-13 of the General Code of the Territorial Authorities provides that in the circumstances set out in the General Code of the Territorial Authorities and the Public Health Code, the Mayor of Paris shall be responsible for ensuring that public highways in the city are kept clean and tidy, for maintaining order at fairs and markets and, subject to the opinion of the Commissioner of Police, for all grants of parking permits to small traders and of permits or licences for erecting stalls on the public highway.

Article L. 2512-13 of the General Code of the Territorial Authorities provides that the Mayor of Paris shall be responsible for ensuring the preservation of State property incorporated into the public property of the City of Paris, and that the power of substitution conferred on the State in the département shall be exercised, in Paris, by the Commissioner of Police.

Section I, Article 1 of the Ordinance of the Consuls of 12 Messidor, Year VIII provides that the Commissioner of Police of Paris shall perform the functions set out therein under the immediate authority of the ministers and shall communicate directly with them about the matters for which their departments have responsibility.

Section I, Article 2 of the Ordinance of the Consuls of 12 Messidor, Year VIII provides that the Commissioner of Police of Paris may republish the administrative rules and regulations and issue orders to ensure that they are complied with.

Section III, Article 21 of the Ordinance of the Consuls of 12 Messidor, Year VIII provides that the Commissioner of Police of Paris shall have responsibility for all matters concerning minor highways, save that an appeal will lie against his or her decisions to the Minister of the Interior.

Section III, Article 22 of the Ordinance of the Consuls of 12 Messidor, Year VIII provides that the Commissioner of Police of Paris shall secure liberty and security on the public highway and shall have responsibility for preventing criminal damage to the public highway, for lighting, for ensuring that residents comply with their obligation to keep the area in front of their houses swept, and for arranging for squares and the perimeters of public gardens and buildings to be swept at the city's expense.

Section 25 of the Law of 9 December 1905 on the Separation of Church and State provides that assemblies for the purposes of worship in premises belonging to or placed at the disposal of a religious association shall be open to the public, shall be exempted from the requirements of section 8 of the Law of 30 June 1881, but shall remain under the supervision of the authorities in the interests of public order, and may not take place until a declaration has been made identifying the premises where they will be held.
Section 26 of the Law of 9 December 1905 on the Separation of Church and State provides that it is prohibited to hold a public meeting in premises habitually used as a place of worship.
The evacuation order for St Bernard's Church was made on the ground that the occupation of the premises was unrelated to religious worship.
The evacuation order for St Bernard's Church was made on the ground that there had been a marked deterioration in the already unsatisfactory sanitary conditions at the church.
The evacuation order for St Bernard's Church was made on the ground that padlocks had been placed on the church exits.
The evacuation order for St Bernard's Church was made on the ground that there were serious sanitary, health, peace, security and public-order risks.

Since 28 June 1996, there had been a marked deterioration in the already unsatisfactory sanitary conditions at St Bernard's Church, the available sanitary equipment being totally inadequate for the long-term use of the premises as a collective shelter.

The number of people present on the premises of St Bernard's Church grew considerably during the last few days before the evacuation order, leading to incidents in the immediate vicinity and notably on the public highway.
The incidents in the vicinity of St Bernard's Church created a risk of behaviour that may result in public order disturbances.
The various movements concerned with the occupation of St Bernard's Church erected barriers on the public highway, across rue Saint-Bruno at the junctions with rue Saint-Luc and rue Jérôme l'Ermite.
The barriers erected on the public highway near St Bernard's Church obstructed the highway, hindering the passage of ordinary traffic and of emergency vehicles.

The church doors and various exits of St Bernard's Church were kept closed, and in some cases padlocked, to enable a filter system to be operated at the only remaining entrance that was permanently accessible.
A barricade formed of barriers chained together was placed between the enclosure railings and the north entrance to the chancel of St Bernard's Church.
The installations at St Bernard's Church (closed/padlocked doors and barricade) constituted a major hazard should an emergency evacuation of the persons present inside the building become necessary.

The activities and movements at St Bernard's Church were totally unrelated to religious worship, which was the exclusive use to which the public building could be put under the law of 9 December 1905.
According to the evacuation order, the situation at St Bernard's Church represented a serious sanitary, health, peace, public-security and public-order risk.
The Paris Court of Appeal held that the occupiers of St Bernard's Church continued their hunger strike for almost forty days and the living conditions of those concerned continued to deteriorate.

The Paris Court of Appeal held that the scale of the demonstrations over several weeks, with barriers being used to obstruct the highway and hinder the passage of vehicles, constituted a risk for security, sanitation, the health of the hunger strikers and public order that justified urgent measures being taken to put an end to the disturbances.
The director of the Paris Mobile Emergency Medical Service (SAMU) was given responsibility on 17 July 1996 for ensuring day-to-day care of the hunger strikers at St Bernard's Church.

The parish priest of St Bernard's Church was reminded of the health hazards to which the occupants were exposed by the precarious living conditions and of the need to allow unrestricted access to the emergency services.
The World Doctors (Médecins du Monde) organisation offered continuous medical assistance in St Bernard's Church.

The World Doctors (Médecins du Monde) organisation made public alarming information on the very serious consequences of the hunger strike for the health of the hunger strikers at the expiration of the medically critical period of forty days.

On 12 August 1996, the ten hunger strikers at St Bernard's Church were evacuated on the basis of Article 223-6 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, solely in order for the men to be given appropriate medical check-ups in hospitals in Paris.
The ten hunger strikers returned to St Bernard's Church of their own accord after being evacuated on 12 August 1996.
Upon returning to St Bernard's Church, the ten hunger strikers immediately declared their intention to pursue their hunger strike action.

Police officers set up a checkpoint at the exit of St Bernard's Church to verify whether the aliens evacuated from the church had documentation authorising them to stay and circulate in French territory.
White occupants of St Bernard's Church were immediately released by police during the evacuation on 23 August 1996.
Police assembled all the dark-skinned occupants of St Bernard's Church, apart from those on hunger strike, and sent them by coach to an aliens' detention centre at Vincennes.
Orders were made for the detention and deportation of almost all of the dark-skinned occupants sent to the aliens' detention centre at Vincennes.
More than a hundred of the occupants detained following the evacuation of St Bernard's Church were subsequently released by the courts on account of certain irregularities on the part of the police.
The police irregularities following the evacuation of St Bernard's Church even extended to making false reports regarding the stopping and questioning procedure.
At 8.20 a.m. on 23 August 1996, a police officer asked the applicant, as she was leaving St Bernard's Church, for documentary evidence that she had leave to stay in France.
The applicant was unable to produce documentary evidence that she had leave to stay in France when asked by the police officer at 8.20 a.m. on 23 August 1996.
At 9.55 a.m. on 23 August 1996, the applicant was taken into custody and informed of her rights pursuant to Articles 63-2 and 63-4 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
The custody measure against the applicant was deemed to have taken effect at 7.56 a.m. on 23 August 1996, when she was stopped.
The applicant refused to speak throughout her period in custody on 23 August 1996.

At 8.15 p.m. on 23 August 1996, the Senior Deputy Public Prosecutor at the Eighth Division of the Paris Public Prosecutor's Office instructed the police officers to bring the applicant before him, with the case file as it stood.
At 1.30 p.m. on 24 August 1996, the applicant appeared before the Paris Criminal Court under the 'immediate summary trial' procedure.
The applicant was accused before the Paris Criminal Court of having entered and stayed in France without being in possession of the documents or visas required by the rules.
The Paris Criminal Court sentenced the applicant to two months' imprisonment, suspended.

The Paris Criminal Court held that the occupation of a place of worship over a period of several weeks in order to contest immigration status and create a movement in their favour in itself constituted an emergency justifying the administrative authority's decision to expel the occupants.

The Paris Criminal Court held that the presence in St Bernard's Church of several hundred people for a period of several weeks, claiming through public statements or spokespersons to be aliens without residence permits or papers, constituted grounds for suspecting that those concerned had committed offences under the immigration rules such that the verification of their identity pursuant to Article 78-2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was justified.

The Paris Criminal Court held that, since a large number of people were stopped at the same time and refused to disclose their identities, the police were not able to carry out an immediate identity check.

The Paris Criminal Court held that the fact that the identity check was not carried out when the occupants were first stopped, but within a reasonable period thereafter given the practical contingencies inherent in an operation of that size, did not render the proceedings defective.

The Paris Criminal Court held that, regard being had to the large number of persons stopped and the circumstances in which the operation was conducted, the applicant was notified of her rights within a reasonable time.
On 23 January 1997, the Paris Court of Appeal, on appeal by the applicant, upheld the sentence of two months' imprisonment, suspended, imposed by the Paris Criminal Court.
On 23 January 1997, the Paris Court of Appeal added an order excluding the applicant from French territory for three years.

The Paris Court of Appeal held that the occupation of a place of worship by approximately three hundred individuals over several weeks, in order to create a movement in their favour and to contest their immigration status, constituted an emergency that justified the administrative authority making an expulsion order without making a prior application to the courts.
The Paris Court of Appeal held that the occupiers of St Bernard's Church continued their hunger strike for almost forty days and the living conditions of those concerned continued to deteriorate.

The Paris Court of Appeal held that the scale of the demonstrations over several weeks, with barriers being used to obstruct the highway and hinder the passage of vehicles, constituted a risk for security, sanitation, the health of the hunger strikers and public order that justified urgent measures being taken to put an end to the disturbances.
On 4 June 1998, the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant's appeal on points of law.
In the proceedings before the courts below, Madjiguène Cissé (the applicant), a Senegalese national, was accused of illegally entering and staying in France.

In the proceedings before the courts below, the applicant duly challenged the lawfulness of the order issued by the Paris Commissioner of Police, without a prior court order, for the evacuation of St Bernard's Church.

The Court of Cassation held that even if the applicant had proved that the evacuation order issued by the Paris Commissioner of Police was unlawful, it would have had no bearing on the outcome of the criminal proceedings against her.

Article 111-5 of the French Criminal Code provides that criminal courts shall have jurisdiction to interpret general or individual administrative decisions or regulations and to determine their lawfulness if the outcome of criminal proceedings pending before them depends on their so doing.
